teaser: A goddess painted to hang in the bathroom suite of the most powerful woman in France.
review_notes:
Dimensions about 108 x 85 cm (Met gives 108.3 x 85.1 cm).
Commissioned by Madame de Pompadour for the bathing apartment of the Château de Bellevue; pendant is The Bath of Venus (National Gallery of Art, Washington).
Pompadour played the title role in a play called La Toilette de Vénus staged at Versailles in 1750: check date.
Diderot's line 'That man has everything, except truth' is from his Salon of 1761.
Entered the Met in 1920 through the bequest of William K. Vanderbilt.
Boucher named First Painter to the King in 1765.
The object at lower right is described as a perfume burner; the tipped vessel as a gilt ewer.

lesson.text: This canvas is about 108 centimeters tall and 85 wide (roughly 43 by 33 inches). That is small for a goddess. It was never meant for a palace hall or a church. It was cut to fit one wall of a private bathing suite, a room where almost nobody would ever be allowed in.

The suite belonged to Madame de Pompadour, the official mistress of King Louis XV and for nearly twenty years one of the people who really ran France. In 1750 she moved into Bellevue, a new château on a hill above the Seine near Paris, and asked her favorite painter, François Boucher, to decorate it.

Around 1750, Pompadour acted on the stage of her own small theater at Versailles, in front of the king. One of her roles was Venus, in a play titled “The Toilette of Venus”. A year later she ordered a painting with the same name.

“Toilette” here means the daily ritual of getting ready: hair, jewels, perfume. For a lady of the court it was half public, with servants and visitors around. Boucher gives the goddess of love the same morning routine, with a staff that happens to have wings.

lesson.title: The staff at work
lesson.text: Three helpers, three jobs. Follow them from the top of the picture down.

spots.title: The hairdresser
spots.text: A cupid pins up her hair, already threaded with pearls and a blue ornament. Venus tilts her head toward him and lets her fingers hang in the air, doing nothing at all.

spots.title: The dove on a leash
spots.text: A white dove rests against her chest, tied with a blue ribbon. The second cupid, at right, holds the other end. Doves were the birds of Venus: they pulled her chariot in ancient stories.

spots.title: The jeweler
spots.text: The third cupid lies on his stomach, feet in the air, pulling strings of pearls out of a dish. Pearls belong to Venus too, since she was born from the sea.

lesson.text: Notice what all three are handling: hair, a bird, pearls. Soft things, shiny things. Boucher is less interested in telling a myth than in painting surfaces, and he sets skin against feathers, silk, gold and metal so that each one makes the others look more precise.

The style has a name, Rococo, the light, curving, decorative taste of France in the first half of the 1700s. The word comes from “rocaille”, the shells and rockwork used to decorate garden grottoes. Shells and scrolls were the signature of the whole period, and one is hiding in this picture.
Somewhere near the bottom, a piece of silver is shaped like a shell. Can you tap it?

spots.title: The shell dish
spots.text: A silver dish with curled, wave-like edges, spilling pearls. Its swirling outline is pure rocaille. The gilded sofa behind Venus is carved with the same curling scrolls.

lesson.text: Rococo art was made for private rooms and private pleasure. Its subjects are light, its lines curl like shells, and its real ambition is to make paint feel like silk, pearl and skin.

Boucher was the right man for it. Besides paintings he designed tapestries, porcelain figures, fans and opera sets, and he gave Pompadour drawing lessons. In 1765 he was named First Painter to the King, the top official post an artist could hold in France.
The picture looks effortless, almost lazy. Its construction is not.

lines.label: A zigzag body
lines.text: Head, torso, thigh, shin: her body runs in a soft zigzag from the top center to the lower right corner. It carries your eye across the whole canvas in one slide.

lines.label: A ring of attendants
lines.text: Cupids, doves and flowers form a loop around her. Wherever you look along it, something leans or looks back toward the middle.

lines.label: The curtain
lines.text: A heavy blue-green silk curtain is pulled aside, tassel and all. You are being shown a scene, the way a stage is revealed at the theater.

lesson.text: That curtain matters. Behind it there are trees, sky and a stone monument, so this bedroom has no back wall. It is a stage set, and Boucher painted real ones for the Paris Opera. The owner of the picture, who had acted the part of Venus herself, would have enjoyed the wink.

Not everybody was charmed. The critic Denis Diderot, reviewing Boucher at the Salon of 1761, wrote: “That man has everything, except truth.” For Diderot, all this pink skin and blue silk was skill wasted on nothing.

spots.title: Her face
spots.text: Round cheeks, small mouth, eyes turned aside. Boucher gave nearly all his goddesses this same doll-like face. Whether it flatters Pompadour herself is something historians still argue about.

spots.title: Two more doves
spots.text: A pair of doves nuzzle at her foot. Their feathers are a handful of quick white strokes over gray, with no outline at all.

spots.title: The perfume burner
spots.text: A gilt bronze vessel with a pierced lid, used to scent a room. Smell is the one sense a painting cannot give you, so Boucher paints the machine for it.

spots.title: The fallen ewer
spots.text: A golden water jug lies on its side among flowers and a blue ribbon. Nobody here is in a hurry to tidy up.

spots.title: Silk
spots.text: The curtain is built from broad dark folds with sharp pale streaks on the ridges. Those streaks are what tell your eye “shiny fabric” instead of wool or velvet.

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: On the stone step, in dark letters: “f. Boucher”, followed by the date. He signs on the furniture of the scene, as if carved there.

lesson.text: The painting had a partner in the same suite, “The Bath of Venus”, which now hangs in Washington. Pompadour died in 1764. Twenty-five years later the French Revolution swept away her world, and Boucher's name became shorthand for everything frivolous about it.

Taste turned again. In the late 1800s American millionaires fell in love with eighteenth-century France, and this Venus crossed the Atlantic. It came to the Metropolitan Museum in 1920 from the collection of the railroad heir William K. Vanderbilt.

So a picture painted for one woman's most private room now hangs where millions pass each year. Was Diderot right that there is no truth in it? Maybe. But it is honest about one thing: the plain, lasting pleasure of looking at beautiful surfaces.

quiz.question: For what kind of room was this painting made?
quiz.explanation: Madame de Pompadour ordered it for her bathing suite at the Château de Bellevue.

quiz.question: Where does the word “Rococo” come from?
options: From the name of a French king
From an Italian word for pink
quiz.explanation: Rocaille was the shell and rockwork used in garden grottoes.

quiz.question: Why are doves and pearls in the picture?
options: They show that the scene is set in winter
They are traditional attributes of Venus
quiz.explanation: Doves pulled the chariot of Venus, and pearls recall her birth from the sea.

quiz.question: What did the critic Diderot say about Boucher?
options: That he could not draw hands
That he had everything except truth
That he was the greatest painter alive
quiz.explanation: Diderot admired the skill and found the result empty.

quiz.question: What does the pulled-back curtain suggest?
quiz.explanation: The scene opens like theater, and Boucher also designed sets for the Opera.

facts.text: Madame de Pompadour once played Venus on stage in front of the king.
facts.explanation: She acted the role in her private theater at Versailles shortly before ordering the painting.

facts.text: The Toilette of Venus is a huge canvas made for a public hall.
facts.explanation: It is only about 108 by 85 cm and was made for a private suite.

facts.text: Boucher only ever worked as a painter of canvases.
facts.explanation: He also designed tapestries, porcelain, fans and opera sets.
